passage: The akhada in Sirsi opened at five, and Divyansh had been there every morning since Class 8. Tonight his father, Mohit, sat on the cot with his arms crossed. "Wrestling won't pay for anything. You will sit for the science stream." Divyansh's chest tightened. He wanted to shout, and he felt guilty for wanting to. Instead he opened his notebook. "Papa, here's my training schedule. Here are my district results. I'll study three hours after practice, and if I don't make the state team by next year, I'll take the science stream." Mohit was quiet for a long time, turning pages. "You wrote all this yourself?" he asked. "Yes." "We'll see," said Mohit, handing the book back, slower than he'd picked it up.

qa.q: What time did the akhada in Sirsi open?
What two feelings did Divyansh have when his father crossed his arms?
qa.a: Defiance and guilt. He wanted to shout but felt guilty for wanting to, so he chose a calm approach.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do that made his case stronger than shouting would have?
qa.a: He showed a plan: a training schedule, district results, promised study hours and a fallback of the science stream, rather than shouting or lying about his studies.

qa.q: How might Mohit be seeing Divyansh's notebook?
qa.a: As proof of real effort and seriousness. He was quiet for a long time, turned pages and asked if his son wrote it himself, so he may be starting to reconsider.

grounding: The protagonist insists on his own sporting path but brings a plan, proof of effort and a fallback instead of shouting.

passage:
Week one. Sarita slammed the door hard enough to shake the calendar. "I'm not quitting athletics for tuition, Maa!" Her mother shouted back that sport would not feed her. Arohi, Sarita's best friend, heard it all over the phone and said nothing. Sarita cried into her pillow, furious and guilty in equal parts.

Week two. Sarita sat on the terrace with Arohi and a notebook. "Shouting isn't working." Together they wrote it out: her district times for the last six months, the coach's letter about the state camp, the evening schedule showing tuition and practice could both fit, and a backup plan to take commerce if she didn't make the state team by Class 12.

Week three. Sarita put the notebook on the kitchen counter after dinner. "Maa, can you read this before you say no?" Her mother read it twice, then said, "Your times really went down this much?" She didn't say yes. But she asked to meet the coach on Saturday.

qa.q: What did Sarita put on the kitchen counter in week three?
qa.a: Sarita put the notebook on the kitchen counter after dinner.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling after the shouting in week one?
qa.a: Sarita felt furious at her mother but also guilty, which is why she cried into her pillow.

qa.q: What went wrong in week one, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Shouting made both sides dig in; a written plan with proof of effort and a commerce fallback gave her mother something real to consider.

qa.q: How might Sarita's mother see the notebook?
qa.a: Her mother may be surprised by the real progress in Sarita's times and reassured that there is a backup plan, which is why she agreed to meet the coach.

grounding: It shows a teen insisting on her own path in sport, feeling guilt and defiance together, and moving from shouting to a plan, proof of effort and a fallback.

passage:
Come, Dilnaz, sit. You think you are the first girl in this family to fight about her future? Let me tell you about Class 10.

I wanted to paint. Not a hobby. A career. My Abba wanted me to be a teacher like my aunt. For months I screamed at him, locked my door, and once I told him I was at a friend's house studying when I was really at the art school on Mall Road. He found out. That lie hurt him more than any shouting.

I still remember my guilt, sitting on the stairs that night. I loved him, and I was so angry with him.

So I changed. I gathered every drawing I'd done that year into one folder. I found out the art school's fees and scholarship dates. I told him I would finish my teacher's training too, as a backup. He took the folder to his room and didn't come out for an hour.

I, Sharmila, did both, and I painted for forty years.

qa.a: The art school was on Mall Road.

qa.q: What was young Sharmila feeling on the stairs that night?
qa.a: She felt deep guilt about lying to her Abba, mixed with love for him and anger at him.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Gathering her drawings in a folder, finding out the fees and scholarship dates, and offering teacher's training as a backup turned things, because it showed a serious plan instead of shouting or lying.

qa.q: What was it like for Abba to find out about the lie?
qa.a: It seems to have hurt him deeply, more than the shouting, because it broke his trust in his daughter.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how as a teen she insisted on an arts path with guilt and defiance, and how a plan, proof of effort and a fallback worked better than shouting or lying.
